Antrum - Gastric POCUS Decision Tool

Patient

Age is needed to classify a CSA of 6–11 cm² with the nomogram (below 6 is always safe, above 11 is always unsafe). Weight is optional for adults and adds a mL/kg safety check.
Gastric ultrasound alone should not decide induction technique. Use it together with the clinical situation (fasting status, urgency, comorbidity and gastric-emptying risk factors, airway assessment) and your own clinical judgement.

Probe position & target view

Pregnant mode: do not scan flat. Scan semi-recumbent at 30–45° with left uterine displacement or left tilt, and in RLD.

Cross-sectional area (CSA)

Free-trace the antrum between peristaltic contractions, outer serosa to outer serosa, at the level of the aorta.

Antral grading

GradeSupineRLDMeaning
0No contentNo contentEmpty stomach. Low risk.
1EmptyClear fluidLikely fasting; small volume (≤1.5 mL/kg). Measure CSA to confirm.
2Clear fluid or air bubblesClear fluid or air bubblesAntrum distended with clear fluid in both positions: likely non-fasting (>1.5 mL/kg). Full stomach.

Website cut-off values
Empty stomach (any one):
  • No content in any position (Grade 0)
  • Clear fluid in RLD only, antrum empty supine (Grade 1)
  • Clear fluid, CSA <10 cm² in RLD (average adult)
  • Clear fluid, estimated volume <1.5 mL/kg
Full stomach (any one):
  • Thick fluid or solid in any position
  • Antrum distended with clear fluid supine and RLD (Grade 2)
  • Clear fluid, CSA >10 cm² in RLD (average adult)
  • Clear fluid, estimated volume ≥1.5 mL/kg

Limitations & special patients

Check before relying on the scan
  • Never call an empty stomach from the supine position alone. Always scan RLD.
  • Gastric ultrasound findings may be inaccurate or uninterpretable in patients with abnormal gastric anatomy (see the four sections below). These patients need extra caution, and clinical judgement cannot be replaced by ultrasound findings alone.
  • Most useful when fasting status is uncertain (non-adherence to fasting, emergencies, unreliable history, delayed gastric emptying e.g. pregnancy, diabetes, severe liver/kidney disease, severe obesity).
Previous gastric resection or bypass
  • Altered anatomy changes antral location and volume relationships. The Perlas formula does not apply.
Gastric band in situ
  • The band distorts the antrum and the normal anatomical landmarks are disrupted.
Previous fundoplication
  • The fundus–antrum relationship is altered and the antrum may be displaced.
Large hiatus hernia
  • The stomach may be partly intrathoracic, making the standard epigastric views unreliable.
Pregnancy
  • Third trimester: the gravid uterus displaces the stomach cephalad. Semi-recumbent positioning (30–45° with left uterine displacement or left tilt) is often more practical than full RLD. Do not scan flat.
  • Use an antral CSA threshold of 9.6 cm² (semi-recumbent) rather than the standard Perlas formula. Tick “Pregnant >28 weeks?” to apply it.
  • A slow deep breath held at end-expiration and slight manual displacement of the gravid uterus can help find the antrum.
Morbid obesity
  • BMI >35: the antrum is found deeper, up to about 7 cm, and is feasible to image in >90% of patients with BMI >40. Use the standard RLD position.
  • The Perlas formula is validated up to BMI 40 and is not validated above this: use qualitative assessment (grading) and clinical judgement. Tick “BMI >40” for a reminder in the result.
  • Obese patients have larger antral CSA and larger absolute fasting volume, but similar volume per kg.
Children (under 18 years)
  • Switch on the pink Paediatric mode button (appears for ages 17 and under). Age and weight are both required.
  • Model (built on 100 fasted children aged 11 months to 17 years): volume = −7.8 + 3.5 × CSA + 0.127 × age in months.
  • Upper limit of normal fasting volume is 1.1–1.2 mL/kg; this app uses 1.1 mL/kg.
  • Under 30 kg a high-frequency linear probe (5–12 MHz) gives the best images.
ICU / ER
  • CSA correlates well with aspirated gastric residual volume. RLD may not be feasible in critically ill patients; evidence in this group is still limited.

Visual reference: classic gastric US findings

Empty stomach (Fasted, Grade 0)With no significant content in the antrum in either position (supine and RLD), the antrum is Grade 0. It looks either flat and collapsed, or rounded to oval with a “bull’s eye” (target) appearance.
Solid, early stage (“frosted glass”)The antrum is distended with thin walls and the content is bright or mixed in echogenicity. The “frosted glass” look, usually soon after a solid meal, comes from air mixed with food along the anterior wall, which blurs the posterior wall and deeper structures.
Solid, late stageContent is heterogeneous and particulate, usually 1–2 hours after a solid meal. Uniform bright content suggests dairy or particulate fluids, and milk curds can look biphasic (bright and dark areas).
Clear fluid (pure liquid)The antrum is round and distended with thin walls, and its contents are anechoic or hypoechoic. Antral size follows gastric volume and looks larger in RLD than supine. A volume assessment can tell baseline secretions from a larger, non-fasting volume.
Fluid with air bubbles (“starry night”)Many air bubbles sit on a hypoechoic background, usually seen soon after drinking clear or effervescent fluids. As with clear fluid, a volume assessment can separate baseline secretions from a non-fasting volume.
